questions.topic: A basis of comparison as a commitment
questions.learningObjective: Identify what selecting a basis of comparison commits an argument to
questions.stem: In her observing log, Wren argues that two novels belong to the same decade because both narrators count their money in the same way.

options.misconception: treats the basis as a label that constrains nothing

questions.explanation: Selecting a basis fixes the dimension on which the two works are judged, so other evidence stops counting. B treats it as decoration, C assumes it can be swapped, and D makes it a shared setting.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish two declared bases for one pair of novels
questions.stem: Two pages in the same log compare the same two novels: one declares theme as the basis, the other declares chronology as the basis.

answer.exemplar: Declaring two bases for one pair of novels splits the comparison into two arguments that do not support each other. Theme and chronology test different things, so a conclusion drawn from one cannot settle the other unless the writer first shows the novels agree on the second basis as well. Otherwise the log offers two verdicts and no ground for combining them.

questions.explanation: Two bases produce two tests, and evidence that settles one test cannot settle the other. The log fails because it never shows the novels agree on the second basis, so its conclusions do not combine.
questions.hint: Ask what each basis can and cannot settle.

questions.topic: The paragraph that states the best objection

questions.stem: In the log, the astronomer devotes one full paragraph to the strongest case against her own reading of the final chapter.

answer.exemplar: A paragraph that states the best objection should name the objection in its strongest form, not a weakened version, then show why the reply holds or concede that it does. questions.explanation: The strongest objection, stated at full strength and answered, shows the writer has tested the claim rather than avoided it. A weak or partial version of the objection would let the conclusion look easy.

answer.exemplar: Both drafts assert a causal link, but only one supplies the warrant the other leaves implicit. options.misconception: treats a common cause as settling any particular closure

options.text: The claim holds, because the notebook records rich workings only for a different seam in the same hill.
options.misconception: assumes the survey covers a different seam without evidence

options.text: The claim outruns the record, because the notebook already holds evidence for a different cause of the closure.

questions.explanation: The survey entry is available evidence for another explanation of the closure, so the claim outruns the record. A, B and C each remove that evidence from consideration by rule rather than by argument.
questions.hint: Ask what the survey already tells you.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The paragraph that states the best objection
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a paragraph that states the best objection

stimulus.body: Objection, stated at full strength: the reading of the ending depends on the preface's single word, which can be read another way. Reply on the page: yes, but the ending's own last page confirms the sense. My note says: the reply never explains why the ending's last page settles the preface, and the objection was about the preface.

questions.stem: What is wrong with the reply as recorded here?

options.text: The reply answers a different question, so the objection about the preface is left standing.
Nothing is wrong, because the ending and the preface belong to the same novel and can confirm each other.
options.misconception: treats shared authorship as shared confirmation

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because the reply quotes the ending and a reader can see the confirmation.
options.misconception: counts a quotation as the substance of an answer

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because the objection is stated in full and stating an objection is the difficult part.
options.misconception: values stating the objection over answering it

questions.explanation: The objection concerns the preface and the reply defends the ending, so the objection is never met. Shared authorship, quotation and the difficulty of stating an objection are not answers to it.
questions.hint: Ask which claim the reply actually meets.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A conclusion that concedes and keeps the claim
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a conclusion can still keep its claim after conceding
questions.stem: A writer concludes that a novel is overrated, granting that its prose is fine while holding that its reputation outruns its ideas.

answer.exemplar: Conceding the prose while attacking the reputation works only if the claim is stated over the right ground. Reputation and ideas are separable, so a book can be well written and badly thought, and a reader who accepts the concession should be left agreeing that the book is overrated on ideas alone. The writer's task is to show that the two verdicts touch different features, since a reader who cannot see that separation has been handed a puzzle rather than a concession.

questions.explanation: The concession and the surviving claim concern different features, so they can coexist, provided the writer marks that separation. Without it, a reader who accepts the prose verdict may reasonably doubt the other.
questions.hint: Mark which features the verdicts cover.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The truth constraint on a reconstructed scene
questions.learningObjective: Apply the truth constraint to a reconstructed scene
questions.stem: A log page reports what a distant observer saw through a telescope, and a later line reports what that observer must have been thinking.

options.text: The second line is fine, because an observer's thoughts can be inferred reliably from what they chose to look at.
options.misconception: believes the choice of subject reveals what a person thought

options.text: The second line exceeds the record, because a telescope image cannot support a report of the observer's thoughts.
The second line is fine, because the notebook already describes the observer's face as it read the display.
options.misconception: assumes the record covers the observer's expression

options.text: The second line is fine, because guessing at a person's thoughts is standard practice in an observing log.
options.misconception: defends the practice by habit rather than by evidence

questions.explanation: A telescope image records light, not a person's thinking, so the second line asserts more than the source can carry. The other options rest on inference, on an assumed record, and on habit.
questions.hint: Ask what the image can actually show.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A basis of comparison as a commitment
questions.learningObjective: Identify what selecting a basis of comparison commits an argument to
questions.stem: A comparison of two novels in the log declares its basis as their differing treatments of inheritance, then argues about prose style.

answer.exemplar: A declared basis is a commitment that fixes which evidence counts, and prose style is not evidence about inheritance however well it is described. The argument therefore drifts: the reader is invited to admire the sentences while the claim remains about a different feature. Either the basis or the evidence has to change, and the writer is the only one who knows which of the two claims is actually meant.

questions.explanation: The evidence offered bears on a different dimension from the basis declared, so it cannot support the claim it accompanies. One of the two must change, and the writer knows which.
questions.hint: Compare the declared basis with the evidence.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two declared bases for the same pair of novels
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish two declared bases for one pair of novels
questions.stem: A notebook entry declares one basis for its comparison of two novels and then, three paragraphs on, argues quietly on a second.

options.text: There is no drift, because a careful writer may legitimately bring in a second dimension as supporting detail.
options.misconception: treats a second dimension as harmless supporting detail

options.text: There is no drift, because the second paragraph repeats the first in concrete form rather than changing basis.
options.misconception: calls a change of basis a repetition

options.text: The drift is the problem: the second argument answers a different question and cannot support the first verdict.
The drift matters only if the two novels disagree on the second dimension, which the entry says they do not.
options.misconception: makes the drift harmless only when the novels happen to agree

questions.explanation: The second argument answers a different question, so it cannot carry the first verdict, whether or not the novels happen to agree. A and B deny the drift, and D makes it harmless by accident of subject.
questions.hint: Ask what the second paragraph answers.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The missing warrant in a cause and effect claim
questions.learningObjective: Locate the missing warrant in a cause and effect claim

stimulus.body: The pigeon is dead and I believe the hawk got it. I have never seen a hawk near the loft, though the neighbours say they have. I am writing it down because it is what I believe, and the note does not say why a hawk would take a pigeon from my roof.

questions.stem: What does the marginal note leave missing?

options.text: The date, since the notebook does not say when the pigeons were last seen at the loft.
options.misconception: looks for a missing date rather than a missing reason

options.text: The neighbour, since a claim like this would need an interview with someone who keeps pigeons.
options.misconception: asks for testimony instead of a stated reason

options.text: The hawk, since the entry names a bird it has never actually seen in the garden.
options.misconception: faults the missing observation rather than the missing warrant

options.text: The warrant, since nothing states why a hawk would take a pigeon from this loft at all.

questions.explanation: The note asserts a cause and never says why that cause would produce this effect, which is the warrant the argument needs. A date, a neighbour and a sighting would each add facts without supplying the missing link.
questions.hint: Ask what reason the note leaves out.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A causal claim outrunning two closures
questions.learningObjective: Assess a causal claim that outruns the available closures
questions.stem: Three notebook drafts disagree about the collapse: one names a single cause, one names two, one argues the second acted only after the first.

answer.exemplar: The three drafts disagree about how many causes the evidence contains, and each answer carries a different obligation. One cause must explain away the rest of the record. Two causes must show they are independent rather than one story counted twice. A conditional cause must show that the condition held, which is the strongest of the three because it explains the sequence the others merely report, and the most exposed, because a condition that cannot be evidenced leaves the draft with nothing at all.

questions.explanation: Each draft carries a different duty: ruling out alternatives, showing independence, or verifying the condition. The conditional draft does the most work and so faces the highest risk of failing its own test.
questions.hint: Ask what each draft must prove.
